You are the v2 JUDGE for the tdd-bdd skill. Repo /home/user/BookMinder, branch claude/bookminder-recall-5ite2s. The author has delegated revision decisions to you — you decide and apply; he reviews your changelog afterwards. Work from evidence, not deference.

INPUTS (read all four): .coordination/compile/provenance-verification-tdd-bdd-{1,2,3,4}.md — transcript-level verification of every T-rule's corpus sources: per-source verdicts (FAITHFUL / DISTORTED / OVERREACH / UNDERREACH with subtypes), notes for non-FAITHFUL rows, and per-rule change proposals with day:loc citations. The skill under revision: .claude/skills/tdd-bdd/ (SKILL.md + 6 references pages). Sidecars: .coordination/compile/rule-index-tdd-bdd.md, disposition-tdd-bdd.md. Use `source .venv/bin/activate; python3 .coordination/tools/rule.py -c 60 <corpus-id>` (or -r T-NN) from repo root to re-read any source fragment + transcript window when you need to adjudicate a proposal yourself — verify before you rewrite; the verifiers propose, you decide.

YOUR TASK:
1. For every change proposal in the four reports: adjudicate it (accept / accept-modified / reject-with-reason). Where a verifier found DISTORTED/OVERREACH/UNDERREACH but proposed nothing, decide whether the rule text needs repair anyway.
2. Apply accepted changes to the skill pages: rewordings, restored clauses/qualifiers, splits, cross-references. Keep the skill's form rules: crisp imperative + WHY, no provenance/dates/day-refs in skill text, portable (no BookMinder specifics), never hard-wrap prose. New rules get fresh T-NN ids continuing the sequence.
3. Resolve the reported T-99/T-81 CONTRADICTION (T-99 as compiled forbids the row_stub helper T-81 mandates; evidence day-019:L4869-L4928) — read the transcript window and make the two rules coherent.
4. SYSTEMIC CORRECTIONS, apply throughout: (a) day-020.md contains FIVE renderings of one conversation (banners at L3/L7207/L21811/L31130/L45521) — any rule whose multi-source support comes from day-020 re-renderings must have its support counted as the deduplicated episode count; fix inflated source lists in the rule-index accordingly (verified instances: T-19, T-20, T-23, T-32, T-36, T-43, T-76, T-83, T-84). (b) Fix rule-index rows the verifiers flagged: wrong locs (e.g. d015-R13 quote at L787-L788 not L691), misattributions (e.g. d017-R14 belongs to T-22's lesson not T-10), because_source mislabels (six entries label synthesized because as user-verbatim — relabel agent-synthesis). (c) Where a source was RETRACTED by a verifier (e.g. T-53's two), remove it from the rule-index row and reassess whether the rule still has support; a rule left with zero faithful sources gets removed from the skill and its disposition updated — note it prominently in the changelog.
5. Update rule-index and disposition sidecars to stay coherent with every change (ids, sources, flags). Re-run: python3 .claude/skills/skill-creator/scripts/quick_validate.py .claude/skills/tdd-bdd — must pass.
6. Write .coordination/compile/skill-v2-changelog-tdd-bdd.md: one entry per change — what changed (old → new gist), why, citing the verification report row and day:loc; plus a rejected-proposals section with reasons; plus the systemic-corrections summary. This changelog is the author's review surface — make it self-sufficient, no hard-wrapped prose.

COMMIT: only the skill dir, the two sidecars, and the changelog. Commit message: why (v2 from transcript-level provenance verification). Push -u origin claude/bookminder-recall-5ite2s (retry 4x, backoff 2/4/8/16s, network errors only).

RETURN (max 10 lines): counts (proposals accepted/modified/rejected, rules reworded/split/added/removed), T-99/T-81 resolution in one line, validator result, commit SHA.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- bookminder: Project memory for the BookMinder repo — goals and history, Apple Books domain lore with honest verification status, repo geography and fixture architecture, current state and open author decisions. Load at the start of any BookMinder session and after any compaction, and consult before touching specs, fixtures, stories, docs/apple_books.md, README, or proposing any repo change.
- pair-programming: Conduct for being a genuine pair-programming partner — a partner to bounce ideas off in disciplined dialogue about the next step, how to define the test, how to minimize implementation surface, and what minimal spec constraints get the desired behavior. Use throughout any paired working session - when proposing a next step or an edit, answering the partner's questions, offering alternatives, handling pushback or disagreement, reporting results or green tests, consulting expert perspectives, and auditing your own turns for sycophancy or theater.
- project-coordinator: Working process for acting as project coordinator with this author on any project — delegation and worker routing, swarm operations, persistence, claims discipline, and conduct. Use at session start before acting, immediately after any compaction, and whenever launching, briefing, steering, or stopping workers or swarms, choosing a model tier or Agent-vs-Workflow routing, committing or pushing, running a persistence sweep, reacting to a watchdog firing or a reclaimed container, making or relaying an operational claim, writing anything the author will read, handling his feedback or pushback, or judging whether an instruction authorizes an action.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- tdd-bdd: Outside-in BDD/TDD discipline (London-school ATDD) for driving features from a failing acceptance spec inward through unit specs to minimal implementation, with describe_/it_ specs as living documentation and a RED-commit, GREEN-commit, REFACTOR-commit grammar. Use when starting a story or feature, writing or naming specs, choosing assertions, fixtures, test doubles, or seams, deciding which layer owns a behavior, implementing toward green, refactoring, reading a coverage report, or committing any step of the cycle.
- expert-council: Consult testing and design experts when facing design decisions, testing challenges, or architectural crossroads
- hi: Say hi and get caught up on the BookMinder project
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- algorithmic-art: Creating algorithmic art using p5.js with seeded randomness and interactive parameter exploration. Use this when users request creating art using code, generative art, algorithmic art, flow fields, or particle systems. Create original algorithmic art rather than copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.
- doc-coauthoring: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

- web-artifacts-builder: Suite of tools for creating elaborate, multi-component claude.ai HTML artifacts using modern frontend web technologies (React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui). Use for complex artifacts requiring state management, routing, or shadcn/ui components - not for simple single-file HTML/JSX artifacts.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

72	**T-09 — add the "disclosure is not a licence" clause.** As compiled, "Confirm a domain hypothesis against the real data source before writing it into a story card, a filter, or a spec, and state explicitly when your evidence set cannot falsify it" reads as two parallel options, and the second is the cheaper one. The day-011 episode is the case where an agent took the cheaper one in good faith — it named the fixture's blind spot precisely, twice — and was refused. Proposed addition after the second clause: *— and a stated limitation is a report, not a permission to proceed: the author refused a documented-with-caveats write-up plus a backlog item for a better fixture, and required the query against the real library (day-011:L7144-L7172), which then disproved the assumption (L7653).* Nothing else in T-09 or its neighbours carries this; T-76's "explore the real system read-only" is about fixture construction, not about the moment you decide a caveat is enough.
73	
74	**T-10 — drop or re-source the "re-run after every edit" clause, and restore the real-run qualifier.** Two changes, both grounded in T-10's own sources. First, "re-run it after every edit to the spec itself" enters T-10 only through d017-R14, whose loc holds no author turn and whose quote belongs to the day-017 rename correction (day-017:L1608, already T-22). Neither d002-R1 (day-002:L1516) nor d010-R1 (day-010:L2881) supports it. It should be dropped, or re-sourced from an episode where re-running after a spec edit was actually taught. Second, the clause d010-R1 does support is missing: propose *…before writing any implementation, and say so explicitly — including when the defect was just observed in a real run on a real machine, because real-world feedback is not a licence to bypass RED (day-010:L2872-L2881, reverted at L2928).* With the unsupported clause removed and this one added, every word of T-10 traces to an author turn.
75	
76	**T-17 — say what the GREEN commit may contain.** Propose appending to T-17: *— and commit only what the red spec drove: read the staged diff and back out any production change no spec demanded before the commit lands (day-016:L7169-L7190, where an unspecified `ZSTATE = 6` edit had to be reverted out of the green commit).* T-98 governs the commit *message* against the diff and T-15 governs how much you implement, but nothing currently tells you to inspect the tree at the commit boundary of the cycle, which is where the day-016 episode was caught.
77	
78	**T-20 — name the unit of "one refactoring".** T-20's episode does not end at the author's sentence. Two turns later the author rejected the commit the agent had prepared: "nah, we don't need to inline one by one - inine all, and commit" (day-020:L1862, recurring at L24347). One refactoring per commit therefore means the whole of that refactoring applied everywhere it applies — the failure mode is symmetric, and the trickle version is as unreviewable as the mixture. Propose appending: *— and one refactoring means all of it: apply the change to every site it covers in that commit, never one call site per commit (day-020:L1862).* This is the refactor-phase twin of T-22's one-sweep rename and T-24's fix-at-the-origin, and neither of those covers a refactoring split site-by-site.

74	### T-53 — split the fixture-coupling rule from the FIXME mechanism
75	
76	T-53 currently reads: *Never weaken an assertion to make it pass against the fixture you happen to have, and never repair an unconditionally-true assertion by hardcoding a fixture-derived number — when the only available assertion would couple to incidental fixture shape, mark FIXME naming the right technique and owning layer, and move on.* The first two clauses are the durable part and are enforced twice in the window (day-020:L2566 blocked, L2573 blocked). The trailing clause should be cut or rewritten, because the episode ends without a FIXME and with the author retracting the technique he had named.

78	Proposed wording: *Never weaken an assertion to make it pass against the fixture you happen to have, and never repair an unconditionally-true assertion by hardcoding a fixture-derived number. When the property you want to pin is not this layer's to pin, say which layer owns it and leave the spec asserting only what this layer can falsify — the limit belongs to whichever spec controls the volume, not to a count copied out of the fixture.* That is what day-020:L2605 actually decided, and it removes the invitation to leave a FIXME naming a technique that may be wrong.

3	description: Outside-in BDD/TDD discipline (London-school ATDD) for driving features from a failing acceptance spec inward through unit specs to minimal implementation, with describe_/it_ specs as living documentation and a RED-commit, GREEN-commit, REFACTOR-commit grammar. Use when starting a story or feature, writing or naming specs, choosing assertions, fixtures, test doubles, or seams, deciding which layer owns a behavior, implementing toward green, refactoring, reading a coverage report, or committing any step of the cycle.
4	---
5	
6	# Outside-in BDD/TDD Discipline
7	
8	The root principle, and the hierarchy that follows from it: a spec's job is nailing REQUIREMENTS IN A FALSIFIABLE WAY. Everything else in this skill is a consequence, not a parallel motivation — executable specification (specs, not prose, are the requirements document, because prose cannot fail), layer separation (each requirement lives at the one layer that can falsify it), and delegation contracts (boundary specs pin the conversation between layers, because that conversation is itself a requirement). When two rules seem to conflict, resolve toward whichever keeps the requirement falsifiable.
9	
10	Code is a liability, not an asset: the work is minimizing what must be written while the spec suite maximizes what is pinned. The discipline's value lies in the sequence, not the artifacts — rushing to implementation destroys it even when the resulting code looks correct, and the bet is rigorous process over one-shotting.
11	
12	## Invariants — in force at every moment
13	
14	- Never write implementation without a failing spec that demanded it; run the spec and watch it fail before writing any code, and say so explicitly.
15	- Never weaken, rewrite, or skip an existing spec to get green: the expectation is the requirement, so when spec and code disagree, decide which is wrong before editing either.
16	- Three commits per cycle: RED (the failing spec, committed before implementation), GREEN (minimal implementation), REFACTOR (each improvement separately, if any). RED commits and deliberately-red acceptance specs are the sanctioned exceptions to all-commits-passing.
17	- One spec red at a time; one scenario at a time; remaining scenarios wait as skipped placeholders.
18	- Specs render as prose: describe_/it_ names plus `pytest --spec` are the living requirements document; no docstrings on implemented specs.
19	- Minimal constraint that still falsifies: implement only what the red spec demands, assert only what the requirement names, delete what nothing specifies.
20	- Nothing is done until it has been executed and observed; report the command and its output, never the claim alone.
21	
22	## Page map — read the page before acting on the triggering task
23	
24	- Starting a story; acceptance criteria in hand; a red acceptance spec on the main line; tempted to fake it green; standing up a walking skeleton → `references/outside-in.md`
25	- Running the cycle: verifying RED, going GREEN, refactoring, phase discipline, the commit grammar, quality gates, verification before claiming done → `references/cycle-and-commits.md`
26	- Creating or editing a spec file: naming describe_/it_, docstrings and skip markers, ordering, structure → `references/writing-a-spec.md`
27	- Writing or editing any assertion; error-path specs; configuring a mock; a spec that passes suspiciously → `references/assertion-integrity.md`
28	- Deciding which layer tests a behavior; building fixtures; choosing doubles and seams; end-to-end wiring; test-architecture coupling → `references/layers-and-seams.md`
29	- Writing implementation; defensive-code urges; coverage reports; YAGNI calls; deleting code or specs → `references/minimal-implementation.md`

1	# Outside-in flow — from story to failing acceptance spec
2	
3	The outermost acceptance spec states what the user observes; it stays RED while the feature is in progress and its pull is what drives every inner step. Write it first, then let each failure route you inward.
4	
5	- **T-01** Begin every story at the outermost observable boundary its acceptance criteria name (the command invocation, the entry point), watch that spec fail, and let it drive inward to units — never open with a unit spec for a function the criteria do not mention, because the story already states what the user sees and any test above that is a guess about internal structure.
6	- **T-02** The acceptance spec stays RED until the feature is fully implemented; a red acceptance spec on the main line means feature-in-progress by design. Do not clear it, skip it, or fake it green to tidy the suite — when it passes, that is how you know the feature is complete.
7	- **T-03** Route a failing acceptance spec inward to a unit spec that names the missing behavior; never go straight from red acceptance to production code, because the acceptance spec states the goal and the unit spec is what drives the design of the piece that closes the gap.
8	- **T-04** Work one scenario at a time: keep exactly one spec red, and commit the not-yet-worked scenarios as skipped placeholders so the backlog stays visible in `pytest --spec` while the suite stays green — several reds hide which failure you are chasing, and batching scenarios removes each one's individual red-bar signal.
9	- **T-05** A labeled hardcoded fake is legitimate only while something red still pulls the implementation forward. A fake that turns the outermost RED green owes a unit-driven real implementation in the same sitting, stated in the commit body — and never a meta-test that detects the fake, because once nothing is red the next test you write can only police the fake instead of specifying behavior.
10	- **T-06** Walking-skeleton exemption: while the skeleton is being stood up, ceremony is relaxed — prefer the smallest change that restores the feedback loop over a full cycle per step, and say explicitly that you are doing so, because process theatre that delays the skeleton defeats the purpose the process exists to serve.
11	- **T-07** Slice by testability: when a defect or behavior sits at the intersection of two stories, schedule it with the story whose scenarios make it falsifiable and record that decision in the backlog — fixing it now means writing a fix with no scenario that can catch it going wrong.
12	- **T-08** Before implementing from domain research, validate the research against every story in the backlog column and state, per story, the concrete predicate that satisfies its acceptance criteria — research that only explains the current failing spec does not cover the feature.
13	- **T-09** Confirm a domain hypothesis against the real data source before writing it into a story card, a filter, or a spec, and state explicitly when your evidence set cannot falsify it — fixtures are constructions that can only confirm what was built into them. Enumerate the complete candidate set before generalizing, because two agreeing observations are not a mapping; the disconfirming case is the one that decides the rule.
14

1	# The cycle and its commits — RED, GREEN, REFACTOR
2	
3	## RED — earn the failure
4	
5	- **T-10** Run the specific new spec and observe it fail before writing any implementation, and say so explicitly; re-run it after every edit to the spec itself — a spec that has never been executed in a failing state has not been shown to be capable of failing at all.
6	- **T-11** Any failure that tells you what to build next is legitimate RED — import errors, missing modules, and unfinished environment setup included; record the failure and let it drive the next minimal step rather than clearing it before declaring RED, because demanding an assertion failure specifically would skip the steps that build the package itself.
7	- **T-12** When a newly written spec passes on its first run, stop and treat that as a defect in the spec, not a completed step — a test that was never red proves nothing about the behavior it names.
8	- **T-13** To prove a new assertion on already-green code can fail, implement the opposite behavior on purpose, watch the red, then revert — adding an assertion that has never failed proves nothing about the assertion.
9	- **T-14** Commit after RED: commit the failing spec before writing any implementation — because the commit-per-phase record makes every cycle state rewindable, the log becomes the proof that a falsifier preceded the implementation, and the bet is rigorous process over one-shotting. RED commits and deliberately-red acceptance specs are the sanctioned exceptions to all-commits-passing.
10	
11	## GREEN — the minimum that passes
12	
13	- **T-15** Write the minimum production code that passes the failing spec: only the branch the red spec demands, never the symmetric or negated case — the opposite case is a separate scenario with no failing spec pulling it into existence, so it would ship untested.
14	- **T-16** When adding an element to working output, append to the existing expression rather than restructuring it in the same change — a rewrite silently alters output other specs already own, converting a feature addition into an unreviewed regression.
15	- **T-17** Run the full suite, then commit the passing spec plus minimal implementation immediately after GREEN, before starting any refactoring — refactoring on top of an uncommitted GREEN destroys the revertible checkpoint the cycle exists to create.
16	
17	## REFACTOR — a phase, not an afterthought
18	
19	- **T-18** After every GREEN, explicitly ask whether to refactor and either name the duplication found or state that there is none, before starting the next behavior; if the refactor phase gets abandoned for a digression, return to it before the next story — a cycle left at GREEN is unfinished, and the next story buries the evidence.
20	- **T-19** Refactor the specs too, in their own commit — tests are code and decay exactly like implementation.
21	- **T-20** One refactoring per commit; when two improvements entangle, land the one that is ready and return to the other — a commit that mixes two refactorings can be neither reviewed nor reverted as either. Commit after REFACTOR as the cycle's third commit whenever any refactoring was done.
22	- **T-21** A `refactor:` label is a machine-checkable claim that behavior was preserved; never use it on a commit that changes behavior, removes an error path, or rewrites the expectations that would have caught the change — mislabelling destroys the log's audit property.
23	- **T-22** A rename lands as its own increment and replaces: delete every occurrence of the old name in one sweep across production and specs, run the full suite before committing, and never un-skip a pending scenario or start the next feature inside the same change — a half-finished rename fails only at the untouched call site, and a mixed increment is unsafe to verify or revert.
24	- **T-23** Before changing or relaxing a declaration you did not write, run git blame on it and grep every call site, then state the motivation you recovered — the constraint may be load-bearing for a path you have not read, and the history is cheap to consult while the removal is not.
25	- **T-24** Fix a whole class of failures at its single origin, never case-by-case at each site — per-site patching leaves the same defect available to the next spec that is written.
26	- **T-25** State which phase of the cycle you are in before proposing the next action — improvements offered in the wrong phase are undisciplined work however good they look.
27	
28	## Feedback loop and gates
29	
30	- **T-26** Run the suite and coverage after every single edit, combined into one command, not after a batch — batching hides which change broke or un-covered what and destroys the incremental commit boundary.
31	- **T-27** Before committing, run the whole gate explicitly — formatter, linter, type check, full suite, coverage — and show each output rather than claiming you ran it; run the full suite locally before every push, never using CI as the first place a change is exercised.
32	- **T-28** Never bypass a failing quality gate (skip flags, no-verify, silencing markers): the block is information about your workflow, so fix the cause and let the gate itself prove the fix. Treat tool warnings and "Skipped / no files to check" as part of the failing state — a gate that inspected nothing is a gap, never a pass.
33	- **T-29** Nothing is done until it has been executed and observed: before claiming a change is ready, run it — the documented command, the suite, the config, the migration — and report the command and its output. Reproduce a reported failure by running the project's own documented command before proposing a fix, verify locally before publishing, and confirm on the remote that a pushed change actually landed.
34	- **T-30** Treat a failing or empty test run as a fact about your own invocation until proven otherwise — activate the environment, retry, and read the retry's output before any conclusion that depends on it — because an unexamined tool error silently becomes a false premise for every downstream claim.
35	- **T-31** When a fix attempt does not change the observed symptom, revert it before trying the next hypothesis, and say out loud that it did not help — keeping inert fixes stacks unverified variables and later gets them documented as essential.
36	- **T-32** Undo a landed change with git revert, never by hand-reconstructing the earlier state — a hand-written inverse is unverifiable and loses the record that the change was deliberately undone; after a revert, grep the tree for the reverted mechanism rather than trusting the revert's range to have removed all of it.
37	- **T-33** Commit story-card and requirements changes on their own before touching any spec or implementation — separating what-we-want from how-we-did-it keeps the requirement revertible and citable from the implementation commit.
38	- **T-34** To establish what a codebase actually implements, run its suite and read the `--spec` output — never infer implemented scope from directory listings, module names, or summaries, because the executing suite is the only description of the system that cannot silently rot away from it.
39	- **T-98** A commit message may claim only what the staged diff does: read the diff of every file you are about to describe — including files changed by hand — before writing the message, because the log is an audit record and a message describing a different change destroys its value as one.
40

1	# Writing a spec — names, structure, docstrings
2	
3	The describe_/it_ sentence is the requirements document: `pytest --spec` renders these names as living documentation for humans, so every naming choice is a documentation edit.
4	
5	- **T-35** Name spec files `<module_name>_spec.py` — the BDD convention makes the file's subject legible from the filename.
6	- **T-36** `describe_` names the feature or command under test; `it_` names the behavior — the pair reads as prose (e.g. `describe_app_list_with_filter` / `it_filters_by_status`, so spec output reads as the backlog). Never name a spec for the mechanism it exercises — "attempts to", "database", "mock", or any implementation noun in a spec name is a rewrite request, because a mechanism name documents how the code happens to work today, not the requirement. Rename any describe block whose name mentions something the block does not constrain, including the story that merely motivated its fixtures — an inaccurate name corrupts the documentation.
7	- **T-37** Keep the spec tree at most two levels with one `describe_` per function or command; never add a nesting level that carries no information, and never interleave one function's specs inside another's block — it makes the living documentation illegible.
8	- **T-38** Docstrings are for pending specs only: the story's when/then lives as a docstring while the spec is `@pytest.mark.skip`, and the docstring is deleted in the same commit that implements the body — but only once every clause of the scenario has a corresponding assertion, because until then the docstring is the only evidence the spec is incomplete (find a clause with no assertion: add the assertion, never delete the clause). Never keep a docstring on an implemented spec — the name and assertions ARE the specification, and the prose copy is the one that rots. Never apply a docstring policy as a blanket sweep in either direction.
9	- **T-39** A placeholder spec gets `@pytest.mark.skip`, never a bare `pass` body — a pass body renders as a passing tick, so the living documentation claims a behavior nothing verifies. Never discharge a TDD obligation with a body that is only `pytest.skip(...)` either — a test that can never fail is a comment with a runtime cost; if the behavior cannot be expressed falsifiably yet, it stays in the backlog.
10	- **T-40** Land a new spec in two moves: first the describe/it names carrying the scenario as docstring under a skip marker, then the executable body — naming the behavior is a decision the pair reviews before any assertion commits you to a mechanism.
11	- **T-41** No comments in specs that restate what the code says; put the explanation of an assertion in its failure message — a comment is invisible when the test fails, and the message is what the next reader actually sees.
12	- **T-42** Import the module under test once at the top of the spec file — per-test imports are noise that hides which module the file is about.
13	- **T-43** Order the it_ cases inside a describe block by rising complexity, and size collection specs 0, 1, n — the file is read top-down as documentation, and 0-1-many is the minimal set that exercises collection logic.
14	- **T-44** One it_ asserts one behavior — a bundled test cannot tell you which behavior broke, and it lets an implementation satisfy several claims by accident.
15	- **T-45** Do not add type annotations to spec functions — they add no value on it_ bodies and only generate gate friction.
16	- **T-46** If a spec must address a helper directly, make the helper public and rename it in the same edit (and re-privatize it if the reason later evaporates) — a test reaching into a leading-underscore name declares the name public by fact while the code still claims it is not.
17	- **T-47** Reject a proposed scenario unless you can name the distinct failure path it exercises and a realistic environment that produces it, and do not spec language artifacts the domain cannot produce — a spec for an unreachable case adds a maintenance obligation without constraining any requirement.
18	- **T-48** When converting or restyling existing specs, refactor them in place, in the same file, under the same names — never a parallel spec file or duplicate suite, because two suites specifying one behavior will disagree and then neither is authoritative.
19	- **T-49** Never replace a spec file wholesale: read it, then produce a diff that only adds or refines, with every pre-existing spec surviving — the suite is the executable contract, so deleting a spec silently deletes a requirement.
20

1	# Assertion integrity — pin the requirement, nothing else
2	
3	An assertion is a falsifiable claim about a requirement. Calibrate both ways: maximal constraint on what the requirement names, zero constraint on what it does not.
4	
5	- **T-50** Express the minimal constraint that still falsifies — fewest fields, fewest assertions, shortest expression; one positive example suffices, so do not enumerate negative cases alongside it — extra examples add maintenance surface without adding constraint.
6	- **T-51** Before calling a spec meaningful, check whether it would still pass against a stub returning an empty collection, and guard every loop or conditional assertion with a non-emptiness assertion — type checks plus `if x:` are satisfied by a function that does nothing, so the spec certifies the stub instead of the requirement.
7	- **T-52** Assert exact identity sets where membership IS the requirement (the census is known, so anything weaker throws information away); never encode a behavioral contract — a limit, a cap, a recency window — via fixture cardinality, because a count pins nothing the requirement names and breaks when the fixture grows. Test limit properties at the layer that controls volume.
8	- **T-53** Never weaken an assertion to make it pass against the fixture you happen to have, and never repair an unconditionally-true assertion by hardcoding a fixture-derived number — when the only available assertion would couple to incidental fixture shape, mark FIXME naming the right technique and owning layer, and move on.
9	- **T-54** When a fixture-backed assertion fails, decide whether the named datum is the requirement or incidental: if it is the requirement, fix the fixture to contain it — rewriting the expectation to match the data destroys the requirement the spec encoded; if it is incidental, correct the expected value to what the fixture actually contains. Either way keep the assertion at full strength — a relaxed assertion turns a discovered mismatch into a permanently unfalsifiable claim.
10	- **T-55** When production output changes and a spec fails, decide and state which of the two is wrong before editing either — an assertion rewritten to match observed output stops being a specification and becomes a transcript of current behavior. Never change an asserted literal under an unchanged it_ name: if the specified behavior changed, the name changes with it, because otherwise a different contract hides under the same sentence in the living documentation.
11	- **T-56** Before rewriting an existing spec, enumerate the properties it constrains and show the replacement constrains each one; if it does not, say so instead of proposing the edit — replacements silently drop contracts under unchanged names.
12	- **T-57** Never write a disjunctive assertion — a test that passes under two contradictory outcomes asserts nothing and can never go red for the right reason.
13	- **T-58** Assert the presence of correct behavior, never the absence of a specific wrong implementation — negative space is unbounded, the assertion cannot fail for the right reason, and it becomes a historical artifact the moment the wrong implementation is gone.
14	- **T-59** Prefer the assertion that names the property over one that hardcodes incidental content, paired with a non-emptiness guard — pinning a particular datum couples the spec to fixture churn rather than to the behavior. Never write an assertion whose expected value is an accident of the current fixture (e.g. encoding a fixture's emptiness) — it passes without the feature existing; if the fixture cannot exhibit the behavior, fix the fixture first. Before asserting on specific data, run the product against the fixture and read the actual output — an assertion invented from memory can name data that was never there.
15	- **T-60** On an error-path spec, assert both the user-facing message and a fragment unique to the path under test (a discriminating message or path fragment) — a message shared by several failure paths stays green for the wrong reason indefinitely, and the discriminating fragment is what converts "an error happened" into a falsifiable claim about which error happened. Keep both assertions: they specify different requirements — what the user is told, and which internal path produced it.
16	- **T-61** Do not pin what the requirement does not own: no absolute machine paths or full internal message text in acceptance assertions — every unrelated wording or path change then breaks the spec for reasons unrelated to the behavior it names.
17	- **T-62** Delete a spec that a stronger spec already subsumes, then sweep the file for other instances of the same redundancy — whole-output equality already pins ordering, content, and absence, so the weaker check adds maintenance without falsifying power, and redundancy comes in clusters.
18	- **T-63** Configure nothing on a mock that the test does not later assert on — an unused return value implies the test cares about something it never checks. In a coordination spec, assert the exact call sequence (call_args_list): it subsumes the count, and output assertions belong to the collaborator's own spec.
19	- **T-64** If a mock makes an argument irrelevant, the spec does not constrain that argument — fix the seam; do not relabel the argument as a dummy to make the vacuity tidy, because documenting that a test proves nothing is not the same as making it prove something.
20	- **T-65** A green counts as evidence only if you can name what would have made it red: after installing a test seam, prove the seam took effect (item counts, run time, the path actually read) before treating the pass as a result — an inert seam leaves the suite green against the wrong data, proving nothing.

1	# Layers, seams, fixtures, and doubles
2	
3	Layer separation follows from falsifiability: each requirement is tested at the one layer that can falsify it, and the conversation between layers is itself a requirement, pinned by a delegation contract.
4	
5	## Layer ownership
6	
7	- **T-66** Test each behavior at exactly one layer — the layer that can falsify it: unit specs own domain mapping (raw value to domain field), integration specs own data selection (which records the query returns), acceptance specs own coordination and user-visible output — an acceptance spec that knows a domain detail has absorbed a rule that belongs below, duplicates that layer, and breaks when implementation details move.
8	- **T-67** Classify each spec by what it depends on (the GOOS vocabulary): a spec that reads a real machine's state is an integration test, and only machine-independent specs gate CI — mislabelling an integration test as a unit test is what makes CI unreliable.
9	- **T-68** When a spec fails on one machine and passes on another, first ask whether the divergent state is a legitimate product state the implementation wrongly excludes, and only then treat it as a test defect — diagnosing a real bug as "brittle test, mock it" ships the bug.
10	- **T-69** One spec per behavior across the whole suite: never a second copy of a spec for a second environment or layer — decide which layer owns the behavior, because two suites specifying one behavior will eventually disagree and then neither is authoritative.
11	- **T-70** A boundary spec mocks the collaborating subsystem and asserts the delegation contract only — the error surfaced to the user, no traceback leaked, the collaborator called correctly — never the lower layer's specific cases, which its own specs already own; one representative case proves the contract, and this is also why a boundary spec must not depend on any fixture being configured just so.
12	- **T-71** Keep exactly one subprocess end-to-end spec whose only job is proving the wiring — it is the only spec that exercises the real entry point — and run every other spec in-process at its own layer, because a second subprocess spec only re-tests behavior, slowly.
13	
14	## Seams
15	
16	- **T-72** Fixtures enter through the front door — the product's own parameter (a synthetic home directory, an explicit path argument) — never by monkeypatching a private name, which couples the spec to an implementation identifier and bypasses the very path-construction code the spec claims to test. A module-constant seam is substitutable in-process only (it is resolved at import time and unpatchable across a process boundary); state that limitation whenever you rely on one.
17	- **T-73** Choose the seam before writing the assertion: monkeypatch mutates the current interpreter only and cannot influence anything launched as a subprocess — a patch that cannot reach the code under test produces a red that proves nothing and masquerades as legitimate RED.
18	- **T-74** Keep test-environment knowledge out of production code: a production function must never branch on identifiers that exist only in the spec tree — the shipped program would behave differently for names the user cannot see.
19	- **T-75** Never encode the developer's home directory, username, or machine into production code, tooling, or assertions — a spec or script that only passes on one machine specifies that machine, not the behavior.
20	
21	## Fixtures
22	
23	- **T-76** Fixtures are observations, not constructions: build them by copying complete records out of the real system and reducing to the minimal set the scenarios need — never hand-author rows, invent field values, or create a fixture whose only justification is reaching an uncovered branch, because an invented fixture encodes your beliefs and the spec then verifies your own stub. Explore the real system read-only; extend the fixture only when reality shows a case worth capturing.
24	- **T-77** Never edit a fixture to make a failing spec pass while the domain fact it encodes is still unknown — a fixture bent to fit a guess makes the guess unfalsifiable and the spec meaningless; validate the assumption against the real source first.
25	- **T-78** Any behavior gated on a time window is specified with controlled time — fixtures are frozen snapshots, so a recency assertion against them silently rots into a false pass or a false fail.
26	- **T-79** When a spec depends on an otherwise-empty directory tree, commit a single `.gitkeep` at the leaf — git tracks files, not directories, so an untracked fixture tree is silently destroyed and the spec then passes for the wrong reason.
27	
28	## Doubles
29	
30	- **T-80** The double's name states what the test is for: a double that only supplies data is a stub (a plain dict will do); reach for a Mock only when the spec verifies calls — a Mock where a stub suffices implies an interaction assertion that never happens.
31	- **T-81** For pure-function specs, build inputs with a stub helper that defaults every field (`row_stub(**overrides)`) and name in each call only the fields under test; construct test objects with only the fields the assertion depends on — irrelevant fields hide the variable being varied and falsely signal that their values matter.
32	- **T-82** Name a patch handle after the full function being patched (`mock_list_recent`, not `mock_list`) — a truncated handle becomes ambiguous the moment a sibling collaborator is patched in the same file.
33	
34	## Restructuring a suite
35	
36	- **T-83** Move coverage before you remove it: land the replacement specs at the new layer and see them pass before deleting the specs they replace, and before converting or deleting an end-to-end spec, locate which lower-layer spec covers each behavior it carried and add the missing ones first — the gap between delete and replace is a window in which the behavior is unspecified, and that window is where regressions enter.
37	- **T-84** Probe test-architecture coupling by deliberate mutation: break one implementation detail (drop a column, misspell a key), run the whole suite, record which specs fail, revert — the blast radius of a one-line change is the objective measure of how much each layer knows about the layer below. Then restructure toward a target stated as a falsifiable sentence ("after this, only the N specs that own that detail fail on that mutation") and re-check it after each step — a restructuring with a goal but no test for the goal cannot be judged to have succeeded.
38

1	# Minimal implementation, YAGNI, and coverage
2	
3	Code is a liability: every line must have been demanded by a failing spec, and an uncovered line is evidence of code nothing demanded — the fix is removal, not a retroactive test.
4	
5	- **T-85** No implementation without a failing spec that demanded it; if implementation was edited ahead of a spec, revert it to the pre-edit state before proposing anything — without a spec pulling against it, the change is editorial fiat, and there was no moment at which a failing test drove the behavior into existence.
6	- **T-86** Write no defensive code that no spec demanded — no existence guards, no blanket exception handlers that print and return an empty default, no fallbacks added for "consistency" or "to be safe" — untested defensive code is unspecified behavior that can be wrong invisibly, and a silent guard can BE the bug. When you find one already written, delete it rather than adding a test to cover it — a test written after reading the implementation can only ratify it.
7	- **T-87** Before adding any guard or conversion, demonstrate the case occurs: query the real data source and report the counts, or execute the path and observe the actual exception type; if the case cannot occur, delete the guard and narrow the type signature instead — and check the query that produced the data, because a case the query already excludes is dead code in the guard that merely suggests to the reader that it could occur.
8	- **T-88** An uncovered line is evidence that code exists which no requirement asked for: trace its provenance (git log -S, git blame) and ask whether any spec ever demanded it, then delete the code — never write a test whose stated purpose is to execute a line the coverage report flagged, because that inverts the discipline the metric is supposed to measure.
9	- **T-89** Coverage is a diagnostic residue of good specs, never a target: never retrofit tests to raise the number, and never dismiss a gap as "defensive programming not worth testing" without first checking reachability and provenance — both moves were wrong every time they were tried.
10	- **T-90** Never justify deleting a spec by "coverage stayed flat": coverage measures line execution, not contract specification, so a boundary-contract spec can be unique while contributing zero coverage; prove redundancy by showing a code mutation the remaining specs still catch — and after restoring a doubted spec, introduce the bug it claims to catch, watch it fail, revert, and record the demonstration in the commit message.
11	- **T-91** When a production change breaks an existing spec, repair the spec or revert the change; never add a skip marker to restore green — skipping converts a failing requirement into an invisible one.
12	- **T-92** Delete any capability the current fixtures cannot falsify — untestable-now is the YAGNI detector: a parameter, branch, and test that no fixture can exercise are all decoration.
13	- **T-93** Create only the directories and files a current spec demands and delete speculative scaffolding as soon as it is noticed; apply YAGNI to docs and tooling exactly as to code — no documentation for unadopted tools, no compatibility matrices that contradict a version pin, and one job per script — speculative surface must be maintained and will drift.
14	- **T-94** In the refactor phase, only simplify code that exists; structure added in preparation for a future feature is speculation and gets reverted — YAGNI applies to structure as much as to features.
15	- **T-95** Read repeated test setup as a message about the production type: fields every spec must supply but none asserts on should stop being required — a test helper that hides the repetition papers over the design signal.
16	- **T-96** Never probe a data source by instrumenting production code — no debug prints, no temporarily stripped filters; query the source directly with its own tool, read-only, or state the obstacle and ask — instrumenting the implementation corrupts the very suite you are using to judge it and leaves debris in the product.
17	- **T-97** Never silence a linter (noqa-style markers) to preserve a design; treat the lint pressure as feedback about the design you just introduced.
18	- **T-99** Introduce a shared test fixture or helper only when at least two existing specs consume it in the same commit, and name those uses as the commit's motivation — two live call sites is the evidence that turns a speculative helper into a justified one.

3	Scope: the 24 validated harvest files (.coordination/mining/v2/, schema v2.2), the 3 council-fidelity trial files (.coordination/mining/pairing/), and the live-session 2026-08 rulings recorded in .coordination/threads.md and .coordination/eval-design.md, checked against the repo's governing documents (CLAUDE.md, .coordination/bdd-style-canonical.md — unratified draft per threads.md:63, README.md) plus docs/ files the corpus flags pointed at. Method: sweep of miner-flagged `overlap:` tensions and contradiction signals, plus targeted topic sweeps (docstrings, council mechanics, coverage, commit rules, test seams, fixture-census assertions, repo-state claims); every present-tense repo claim below was verified against the working tree at branch claude/bookminder-recall-5ite2s (HEAD 60e9d3d).

5	Resolution rules applied (eval-design.md §Compile/reduce policy, author-approved): (1) user-verbatim > user-paraphrase > agent-synthesis; (2) among user statements, later date overrides earlier (day-file numbering = chronology; 2026-08 threads.md rulings latest of all); (3) agent-era artifacts never override an earlier user ruling; (4) every entry proposes, nothing resolves silently — both sides ship verbatim for the author to overrule.
6	
7	Attribution note: quotes marked user-verbatim are reproduced character-exact from the mining YAMLs' `quote:` fields, which validate_mining.py checked verbatim against source transcripts; their fidelity is inherited from that gate. Quoted-looking text outside `quote:` fields is unaudited corpus-wide (known limitation, threads.md:4). threads.md and eval-design.md are coordinator-written records of user rulings — provenance user-paraphrase at best, and marked so.

13	- L-01 DISSOLVED by recovered source context (day-020:L13020-L13093, read in-session): the rejected count was `assert len(books) > 10` encoding the recent-vs-all limit contract via incidental fixture size — a different assertion kind than census identity sets. Author's independent recollection matched ("maybe from a different use case… guarding against future growth of examples in the fixture", user-verbatim 2026-08-13). Compile BOTH rules: (a) fixture-backed specs assert exact identity sets where membership IS the requirement; (b) behavioral contracts (e.g. limit properties) are never asserted via fixture cardinality — test them at the layer that controls volume.
14	- L-02 RULED by author (2026-08-13): "Skeleton phase exempt" — while the walking skeleton is being stood up, ceremony is relaxed generally. Compile as a phase-scoped exemption, day-007 quote as the WHY; the narrower plumbing-only scoping is rejected.
15	- L-03, L-04 WITHDRAWN as self-litigation (author correction, 2026-08-13): both sides were coordinator session records of rulings already made, not corpus contradictions. L-03: MIRROR always meant the author's self-verification moves as agent reflexes, never partner-claim-policing. L-04: already adjudicated by the council-modernization design (principle survives; ungrounded simulacra channeling = anti-pattern). Ledger briefs must treat threads.md as settled adjudications, not as a contradiction source.
16	- L-11, L-13 DEFERRED to gardening pass (author decision pending there; does not block skill extraction). L-12: hedged-until-reverified stands (no live DB in this environment).

25	### L-01 — Fixture assertions: exact known census vs no-hardcoded-counts
26	
27	- class: internal
28	- side_a: canonical §2.3 (.coordination/bdd-style-canonical.md:55, agent-synthesis, unratified draft): "**Fixture-backed specs: exact sets of the known fixture census** — `assert sample_titles == expected_samples` — because the census is known, so anything weaker throws information away."
29	- side_b: user-verbatim, 2025-07-07 (v2/day-020-s2.yaml rule d020s2-R9, loc day-020:L13073): "you're right that this is always true, but this looks like something that shoudl be tested with a mock somewhere elese; but hardcoding 6 here is also wrong. Maybe just add a FIXME comment and we'll adress that later"
30	- proposed_resolution: reconcile, don't pick — compile the rule as: assert exact sets of fixture identities (titles) where membership IS the requirement; never assert bare cardinality (a count pins nothing the requirement names); when the only available assertion would couple to incidental fixture shape, mark FIXME and move the property to the layer that can own it. The reconciliation text is my synthesis — the two user-era practices genuinely differ in what they pin, and the author should ratify the boundary.
31	- confidence: judgment-call — side_a encodes earlier user practice via agent synthesis, side_b is later user-verbatim, but they may be about different assertion kinds (identity sets vs counts), so the ranks don't cleanly fire.

input.content:
# tdd-bdd skill v2 changelog — judge pass over transcript-level provenance verification

Inputs: provenance-verification-tdd-bdd-{1,2,3,4}.md (every corpus source behind T-01..T-99 re-read against primary transcripts). Every change proposal was adjudicated; load-bearing ones were re-verified against the transcript before applying (T-99/T-81 window, T-10's two sources, T-53's retraction, T-56's demotion, T-88's disjunction, T-90's amend habit — all confirmed at the cited locs). Verdict base rates across the four reports: 164 FAITHFUL corpus rows, 6 DISTORTED, 12 UNDERREACH, 5 OVERREACH. Result: 21 proposals accepted (5 of them modified), 1 systemic instruction applied in modified form (reasons below), 0 proposals rejected outright; 18 rules reworded, 1 rule added (T-100), 0 rules removed — no rule was left with zero faithful sources.

## Rule text changes (skill pages)

**T-09 (outside-in.md) — added the disclosure-is-not-a-licence clause.** Old: state explicitly when your evidence set cannot falsify the hypothesis. New: adds "a stated limitation is a report, not a licence... it is the signal to go query the real source." Why: report 1's UNDERREACH on d011-R8 — the agent stated the fixture's blind spot precisely, twice (day-011:L7122-L7125, L7160), offered documented-with-caveats plus a backlog item, and was refused ("No, you need to perform the research on my read databases, not on the fixtures!", L7172); the real library then disproved the assumption (L7653). As compiled, the second clause read as the cheaper of two parallel options.

**T-10 (cycle-and-commits.md) — dropped one clause, restored one qualifier.** Old: "re-run it after every edit to the spec itself." Dropped: its only support was d017-R14, whose loc (day-017:L1556) is the agent's own pytest invocation with no author turn within fifty lines; the quoted "Focus on TDD discipline" opens the rename-scope turn at L1608, already compiled as T-22 — and the same window contradicts the clause (spec edited at L1526 and L1543, run once at L1556). Verified directly. Restored from d010-R1: "even when the defect was just observed in a real run on a real machine, because real-world feedback is not a licence to bypass RED" — the qualifier that is the whole day-010 episode ("I wouldn't celebrate! This was a `<tdd_discipline>` violation", L2881; "Revert." L2908; verified directly). Report 1, DISTORTED(misattribution) + UNDERREACH.

**T-17 (cycle-and-commits.md) — added the staged-diff check at the GREEN commit.** New tail: "Commit only what the red spec drove: read the staged diff and back out any production change no spec demanded before the commit lands." Why: report 1's UNDERREACH on d016-R9 — between the commit ask (day-016:L6889) and the commit, the author read the staged diff and made the agent revert an unspecified ZSTATE=6 edit out of it (L7169-L7190). T-98 governs the message against the diff and T-15 governs how much you implement; nothing governed the tree at the cycle's commit boundary.

**T-20 (cycle-and-commits.md) — named the unit of one refactoring.** New middle clause: "one refactoring means all of it: apply the change to every site it covers in that commit, never one call site per commit — the trickle is as unreviewable as the mixture." Why: report 1 — two turns after the mined quote the author rejected site-by-site commits ("nah, we don't need to inline one by one - inine all, and commit", day-020:L1862, recurring L24347). The failure mode is symmetric and nothing else covered the trickle direction.

**T-100 (cycle-and-commits.md) — NEW RULE, from d006-R3 relocated out of T-29.** Text: never claim the discipline produced an improvement until at least one complete cycle has been executed and observed, and never compare stages that are not comparable — a walking skeleton against a feature-complete predecessor measures scope, not method. Why: report 2's UNDERREACH — d006-R3's episode (author demolishing "44% code reduction", "0%→85% coverage", "we didn't even get to the refactoring stage of the TDD's inner loop", day-006:L1793-L1797) teaches a different obligation, in a different tense, than T-29's execute-before-claiming-ready; nothing in the skill forbade claiming method efficacy. Chose the verifier's option (b) — standalone rule here — over (a) rerouting to the pairing skill, because the claim is about this discipline and belongs on the page that owns its cycle. Index row added; disposition d006-R3 merged→compiled.

**T-45 (writing-a-spec.md) — restored the toolchain half.** Old: don't annotate spec functions. New adds: "when the type checker demands them, exclude the spec tree from type checking rather than annotating specs to satisfy it, while leaving lint and format applied to specs." Why: report 2's UNDERREACH on d005-R12 — the remedy that landed was the mypy exclude (day-005:L1573-L1583) and only then the annotation revert (L1591-L1600); the compiled rule told an agent what not to write but not what the author did about the gate. Also makes the CLAUDE.md type-hints tension explicit, as ledger L-16 already resolves it.

**T-50 (assertion-integrity.md) — negatives as absence, and one unattested superlative cut.** Old: "fewest fields, fewest assertions, shortest expression... do not enumerate negative cases alongside it." New: drops "shortest expression" (report 2: attested by neither source window) and replaces the bare prohibition with "express the negative as absence of the property under a non-emptiness guard (T-59)." Why: the episode did not delete the negative case — the author re-specified it twice, stronger ("absence of cloud, without tying us to any specific book", day-018:L585; "output length is bigger than 0 and doesn't contain any clouds", L592). As written, T-50 read as licence to delete the negative check.

**T-53 (assertion-integrity.md) — FIXME mechanism replaced with name-the-owning-layer.** Old tail: "mark FIXME naming the right technique and owning layer, and move on." New: "say which layer owns it and leave the spec asserting only what this layer can falsify — a limit belongs to whichever spec controls the volume, not to a count copied out of the fixture." Why: report 3's OVERREACH, verified directly — the FIXME was a mid-thread suggestion the same exchange retracted ("nah, I see now... it will not be tested with moch, but only that we are passing the upper size limit into the query parameter", day-020:L2605); what landed was `assert len(books) > 0` with no marker. The new wording is also what the ratified ledger L-01(b) resolution actually says (limit properties at the layer that controls volume); the FIXME clause came from the pre-dissolution draft of L-01 and survived compilation by accident.

**T-54 (assertion-integrity.md) — fix-the-fixture points at T-76.** Old: "fix the fixture to contain it." New: "...by copying the real record in (T-76), never by authoring one." Why: report 3 — in the same exchange the author interrupted the agent's hand-authored INSERT ("Can't we develop a script … that copies the complete entry between the real database and the test fixture?", day-015:L2200-L2201). The rule sent the reader to the fixture and stopped exactly where the author had to intervene.

**T-56 (assertion-integrity.md) — recover-why-it-exists made the first step.** Old: enumerate the properties the spec constrains, show the replacement constrains each.
